title: Data-driven decisions & data ethics
source: Session 1 handout (DDM 26/27) – Wedel & Kannan (2016), Sivarajah et al. (2017), Mazzei & Noble (2017), Zuboff (2019), GDPR/DSA, Susskind (2022)
tagline: Data does not replace intuition – it tests it. This session gives you the vocabulary for everything that follows: what data is, which question each type of analytics answers, how firms earn money with data – and where the ethical and legal limits are.
goals: explain the **5 Vs** of Big Data and structured vs. unstructured data
match a business question to **descriptive, diagnostic, predictive or prescriptive** analytics
choose between **exploratory, descriptive and causal** research
name the three ways firms create value through data (**tool, industry, strategy**)
explain **surveillance capitalism** and the main features of **GDPR** and the **DSA**

sections.heading: Data and intuition
sections.lead: Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph: you need both. Data can tell you with certainty that the red button beats the blue one by 2.7 % – but it will never tell you which of the 16.7 million colours to test.

sides.label: Intuition / experience
points: Generates the ideas and hypotheses worth testing
Fast, but prone to bias
Cannot prove that something works

sides.label: Data
points: Validates or rejects assumptions
Quantifies effects (e.g. +2.7 % clicks)
Cannot tell you what to test in the first place

blocks.note: Goal of a data-driven culture: less “I think …”, more “The data shows …” – data informs intuition, it does not replace it.

blocks.title: Framework to understand data & marketing analytics (adapted from Wedel & Kannan, 2016)

items.label: Types of data
items.text: Structured vs. unstructured, Big Data

items.label: Analytics & methods
items.text: From descriptive statistics to machine learning

items.label: Implementation
items.text: Bringing data and analytics into the organisation

items.label: Applications
items.text: Personalisation, CRM, marketing mix – always framed by privacy & security

Information, especially facts or numbers, collected to be examined and used to help decision-making – or information in electronic form that can be stored and used by a computer (Cambridge Dictionary).

The explosion in the quantity (and sometimes quality) of available and potentially relevant data, largely the result of recent advances in data recording and storage technology (Diebold, 2000). In short: **Big data is … data.**
The process of examining datasets to draw conclusions about the information they contain, increasingly with specialised systems and software.

items.label: Volume
items.text: Sheer amount of data

items.label: Velocity
items.text: Speed at which data is generated and must be processed (real time)

items.label: Variety
items.text: Many formats: numbers, text, images, video, sensor data

items.label: Veracity
items.text: Trustworthiness and quality of the data

items.label: Value
items.text: Only worth it if it creates business value

sides.label: Structured data
points: Fits into rows and columns (tables, databases)
e.g. transactions, prices, age, CRM records
Directly analysable with statistics

sides.label: Unstructured data
points: No predefined format
e.g. reviews, social posts, images, videos, call recordings
Needs sense-making first (text, data & visual mining → Session 4)

blocks.text: Memory hook for the 5 Vs: **3 technical Vs** (Volume, Velocity, Variety) describe the data, **2 business Vs** (Veracity, Value) ask whether you can trust and use it.

sections.heading: Four types of analytics
sections.lead: The four types build on each other: from information (what happened) over insight (why) to decision and action (what to do). Each answers a different question (Sivarajah et al., 2017).

steps.label: Descriptive
points: KPIs, dashboards, reports

steps.label: Diagnostic
points: Drill-down, correlation, experiments

steps.label: Predictive
steps.text: What is likely to happen in the future?
points: Forecasts, regression, ML

steps.label: Prescriptive
steps.text: So what? Now what? What is required to do more?
points: Optimisation, next-best offer

blocks.note: Value and complexity increase from left to right.

blocks.title: Spot the type in an exam question
head: Question
Type
rows: “How many units did we sell in Q3 per region?”
“Why did sales in Italy drop after the price change?”
“How many customers will churn next month?”
“Which offer should we send to which customer to maximise profit?”

sections.heading: Three research types
sections.lead: How clearly the problem is defined decides which research design you need – moving from descriptive to diagnostic analytics.

head: Exploratory
Descriptive
Causal
rows: Aware of problem – “Who buys our (competitors') products?”
Clearly defined – “Will customers buy more after a website change?”
Flexible, versatile; often the front end of the research design
Prior specific hypotheses; preplanned and structured
Manipulate one or more independent variables; control other variables
Expert surveys, pilot surveys, qualitative research, secondary data (qualitative)

blocks.title: Correlation is not causation
blocks.text: Only **causal research (experiments)** lets you claim that X causes Y. Surveys and observational data show associations. This idea comes back in A/B testing (S6) and regression (S9–S10).

sections.heading: How companies create value through data
sections.lead: Mazzei & Noble (2017) distinguish three levels – from using data internally to building the whole business model on it.

steps.label: Data as a tool
steps.text: Active data collection and internal analytical capabilities improve specific functions: product development, marketing, sales, distribution, customer service.

steps.label: Data as an industry
steps.text: Firms sell big-data products and services to others: technology and data-as-a-service; intensive in technical know-how.

steps.label: Data as a strategy
steps.text: Big data drives competitive strategy, new business models and ecosystems built on accumulated data – e.g. **Rolls-Royce** (engine data → service model).

blocks.title: How AI shifts data-driven marketing

sides.label: Starbucks – Deep Brew
points: Reinforcement learning selects the next-best offer and learns from every response
Implemented in the app, designed for heavy users
From segment-based campaigns → individual real-time journey
From short-term response → long-term value maximisation

sides.label: Sephora – Virtual Artist & Beauty Advisor
points: Smart skin scan recommends products; AI agent discusses routines, books appointments, offers discounts
From reactive personalisation → autonomous digital sales agent
From A/B testing → continuous real-time adaptation
From campaign-based promotion → 1:1 digital selling

blocks.note: Think about the data inputs: purchase history, time, location, weather, app behaviour (Starbucks); skin scans, preferences, chat history (Sephora).

items.text: A new economic order that claims **human experience as free raw material** for hidden commercial practices of **extraction, prediction and sales** – a logic in which producing goods is subordinated to a global architecture of **behavioural modification**, with unprecedented concentrations of wealth, knowledge and power.
The gap between what people think they should do to protect their privacy and what they actually do.

steps.label: Extraction
steps.text: Behavioural data collected, often without real awareness

steps.label: Prediction
steps.text: Algorithms forecast what we will do

steps.label: Modification
steps.text: Behaviour is nudged to make predictions come true

items.label: Shoshana Zuboff
items.text: Surveillance capitalism as a “coup from above” that threatens human autonomy and market democracy.

items.label: Byung-Chul Han
items.text: Big Data is a **psychopolitical instrument**: people are degraded to profitable data sets, guided “like puppets on algorithmic strings”.

items.label: Cathy O'Neil
items.text: The era of **blind faith in algorithms** must end – algorithms embed opinions and can reinforce inequality (“Weapons of Math Destruction”).

sides.label: Physical privacy
points: Violated when a person's efforts to seclude or conceal themselves are frustrated

sides.label: Information privacy
points: Disturbed when data, facts or conversations a person wishes to keep secret or anonymous are acquired or disclosed

items.label: Clear language
items.text: Privacy policies in plain, straightforward language

items.label: Consent
items.text: Affirmative consent – silence is no consent

items.label: Transparency
items.text: Inform about transfers outside the EU, purpose of use, algorithmic decisions

items.label: Stronger rights
items.text: Breach notification, data portability, access to a copy, right to deletion

items.label: Enforcement
items.text: European Data Protection Board interprets, decides and imposes fines

blocks.title: Did GDPR work? (Kollnig et al., 2021)
blocks.text: In ~2 million Android apps, third-party tracking changed **only a little** after GDPR – and ownership of trackers became **more concentrated** (risk of user-data monopolies, “gatekeepers”).

blocks.title: Digital Services Act (EU, from 2023)
items: Purpose: a basic law for the internet – rules on cookie banners, online advertising, deletion of illegal content, transparency of algorithmic decisions
Institutions: new Digital Services Board with Digital Services Coordinators in member states
Scope: all firms offering digital services in the EU (internet & hosting providers, cloud, social networks, messengers, marketplaces); **strictest rules above 45 million monthly users**

blocks.title: Susskind – four principles of a Digital Republic

items.label: Preservation
items.text: Preserve the role of the state (a say in company standards that affect its users)

items.label: Domination
items.text: Identify and reduce unaccountable imbalances of power (e.g. Musk's Twitter takeover)

items.label: Democracy
items.text: Moral and civic values should be reflected in technological innovation

items.label: Parsimony
items.text: The state should restrain others only where strictly necessary

recap: Big Data = 5 Vs: **Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value**; data is structured or unstructured.
Research: **exploratory** (ambiguous problem, qualitative) → **descriptive** (surveys, panels) → **causal** (experiments). Correlation ≠ causation.
Value through data: **tool → industry → strategy** (Mazzei & Noble); AI moves marketing to individual, real-time, autonomous selling.
Surveillance capitalism: **extraction → prediction → sales → behavioural modification** (Zuboff); critics Han and O'Neil.
GDPR: clear language, consent, transparency, stronger rights, enforcement – but limited effect on tracking; DSA: strictest rules > 45 m monthly users.
exam: Session 1 is **not** used for calculation exercises – but its concepts regularly appear in the **true/false part** (analytics types, research types, data ethics, GDPR).
Typical T/F: “Causal research is flexible and the front end of the research design” → false (that is exploratory research).
Be able to classify a question into one of the four analytics types and one of the three research types.
traps: Descriptive **analytics** (what happened) and descriptive **research** (who buys?) are different classifications.
Silence or pre-ticked boxes are **not** consent under GDPR.
Big Data is not only about volume – veracity and value matter just as much.
